paragraphs.original: \item Does knowledge distillation from a fine-tuned teacher model into a nano-scale student model yield higher detection accuracy than fine-tuning the same student directly on the wildlife dataset, given the domain shift from COCO-style classes to $225$ mammal species?

\item Which synthetic-image generator produces the most useful training data for this domain, and do the two criteria available before any detector is trained, apparent visual realism and per-image price, predict that ranking?

\item How does the composition of a class's training data, from synthetic images alone through a large pool of real photographs, affect detection accuracy, and does accuracy measured on the mixed test set hold up on the real test set alone?

\item How far is a nano-scale detector from real-time inference without quantization or any other compression step, and how much latency and model size does it save against the two-stage ensembles, measured on a target-adjacent proxy device?

Direct fine-tuning is the better recipe for this student. It leads the distilled student in all $17$ cells of \Cref{tab:kd-vs-direct}, at a mAP of $0.529$ against $0.479$ over all bands, and the margin is widest on Band A, at $0.300$ against $0.239$, where the teacher's soft targets were expected to help most because the supervision there is synthetic and thin. The teacher's class distribution added nothing to the training signal that the labels did not already carry, and the Band A margin suggests that where it deviated from them, it did harm. \Cref{sec:limitations} argues why this pairing and this form of distillation could contribute so little. The comparison ran one response-based configuration, at $T = 4$ and $\alpha = 0.5$, with one teacher at a parameter ratio of roughly $70$ to $1$, and the two runs differed in effective batch size (\Cref{sec:results_kd_basic_comparison}). It rules out a benefit from that configuration and does not rule out knowledge distillation for this domain.

paragraphs.original: \texttt{gpt-image-2} at its cheapest quality tier, prompted under the unabridged \texttt{full} regime, produced the most useful training data of the twelve cells, at $0.134 \pm 0.014$ mAP (\Cref{tab:generator-ranking}). Neither of the two criteria available before a detector is trained predicted that ranking. The generator selected for the production dataset on apparent realism ranks third and trails the leader by roughly $28\%$ under the same prompt regime, and the two \texttt{gpt-image-2} tiers, priced $2.9$ times apart, are separated by $0.008$ mAP. What does predict the outcome is how much the generator is told. Compressing the prompt roughly halves downstream accuracy for both models tested, at $-45\%$ and $-48\%$ (\Cref{tab:prompt-length-ablation}), a larger effect than most differences between generators. Earlier work found the same, in that bare class-name prompts yield poor training data and alignment with the target classes, not visual fidelity, is the variable that matters \cite{aziziSyntheticDataDiffusion2023}. The ranking holds for the data-rich classes only. On the six rare classes every cell stays below $0.05$ average precision, so the executed evaluation axis cannot order generators for the classes that motivated generating images (\Cref{sec:results_per_class_structure}).

paragraphs.original: A qualitative observation belongs beside these measurements. The stripe patterns in the generated zebra images of \Cref{fig:appendix-gallery-plains-zebra}, set against the photographed animals of \Cref{fig:zebra-species}, reach a level of detail that the author could not distinguish from photographs by eye. This was not measured, since the blind rating rubric was not run, but it marks how far image generation has moved. Species detail of this kind was out of reach of generators a few years ago, and the present open-weight models appear to stand roughly where the proprietary services stood then. What is measured is the remaining gap, since under each model's best prompt no local model reaches any API service (\Cref{tab:generator-ranking}). Supplementing a fine-grained species dataset with generated images has become feasible only recently, and it depends on that progress continuing.

paragraphs.original: Half of a small real training set can be replaced by generated images without measurable loss, and the whole of it cannot. At the matched budget of $200$ images per class, Band B trains on $100$ real and $100$ synthetic images and Band C on $200$ real ones, and the two bands score $0.588$ against $0.591$ for \textit{YOLO26n} and $0.638$ against $0.639$ for the fine-tuned teacher, with \textit{YOLOv5s} the exception at $0.341$ against $0.386$ (\Cref{tab:band-grid-real}). Band A, trained on synthetic images alone, reaches $0.300$ for the primary detector, roughly half of what the same budget of real photographs achieves. That shape agrees with the finding that a classifier trained on generated images alone needs about five times as many of them to match real images of the same classes \cite{heSyntheticDataGenerative2023}. Both comparisons rest on single runs over bands that hold different species, so they are directional. The generator comparison, designed independently, reaches the same boundary, since it ranks generators for classes with real photographs and cannot for classes without them (\Cref{sec:results_band_granularity}). Generated images extend a small real pool and do not replace one.

paragraphs.original: Where the remaining accuracy is lost is the second learning of the band grid. The primary detector recovers $0.798$ of the animals at $100$ detections against a mAP of $0.529$ (\Cref{tab:headline-coco12}). For every model, the drop from class-agnostic detection to naming a look-alike group is $16$ to $22$ times the further drop to naming the species within it (\Cref{tab:granularity-gaps}, computed on the mixed test set like the confusion counts below). The errors cross look-alike groups instead of staying inside them. Within the groups, confusion is common but concentrated, with $19.3\%$ of correctly grouped detections misnamed and five of the $30$ groups carrying $60\%$ of those errors, and it runs one way, as with the $1{,}545$ Asian elephants labelled African against $9$ in the reverse direction (\Cref{sec:results_lookalike_confusion}). Naming the species, not finding the animal, is where a nano-scale detector loses its accuracy on this taxonomy, and a detector that could fall back to a coarser name would keep much of what is lost (\Cref{sec:further_work}).

paragraphs.section: Question $4$: Latency and Model Size Without Compression
paragraphs.original: The nano-scale detector runs in $423$\,ms per frame on the proxy CPU at full precision, against $949$\,ms for \textit{YOLOv5s} (\Cref{tab:embedded-latency}). The two ensembles set the scale. Composed estimates put the teacher ensemble at roughly $35$\,s per frame and the pairing of \textit{YOLOv5s} with the same classifier at roughly $5.4$\,s, so \textit{YOLO26n} is $83$ and $13$ times faster with $71$ and $22$ times fewer parameters, at $0.070$ mAP below a teacher figure that is itself an upper bound (\Cref{sec:results_embedded_benchmark}). No compression pass was applied, so these figures bound the latency from above, and the accelerated integer path of the target remains unmeasured. The measurement confirms the argument of \Cref{sec:lit_md_speciesnet}: a two-stage ensemble of this size does not fit a mobile system-on-chip, and a single detector trained on the full taxonomy reaches two orders of magnitude less latency and size at a small loss of accuracy.

paragraphs.section: Question $4$: Latency and Model Size Without Compression
paragraphs.original: The size of that gain was not expected, and neither was where it came from. \textit{YOLO26n} is at once the smallest, the most accurate and the fastest of the detectors measured, $2.8$ times smaller than \textit{YOLOv5s} and $0.122$ mAP ahead of it, although both were trained on the same data under the same schedule. Two generations of architectural progress in the same model family outweighed anything that tuning the older architecture could plausibly have returned. The same pattern is visible across the field at present, with large language models as the most visible case, in that adopting the newest iteration often yields more than investing the same effort in the previous one. That is a general observation and not a measured result of this work, but the measured part, a newer nano-scale model outperforming a larger older one on every axis, is the strongest reason to repeat such comparisons as new generations appear.

paragraphs.original: The distillation tested here transfers only the teacher's final class distribution, the least informative of the forms surveyed in \Cref{sec:lit_knowledge_distillation}, and a confident teacher's distribution is close to a one-hot label. Two properties of this setting weaken it further. The ground-truth species labels were produced by the same classifier pipeline that later became the teacher (\Cref{sec:speciesnet_matching,sec:teacher_finetuning}), so the soft targets largely repeat the hard labels and deviate from them mostly where the teacher is wrong. And a species label has one right answer per animal. In domains where a prediction has no single correct outcome, such as the behaviour of other road users in driving, a teacher's distribution over plausible outcomes carries information a hard label cannot, and a strong teacher can be expected to help a student far more there than it could here. One configuration and one pairing were run, so a stronger form of distillation on this task remains untested.

paragraphs.restored: This study provides a measured map showing where generated imagery assists a fine-grained wildlife detector. It also presents evidence that a nanoscale, single-stage detector can resolve a $225$-species taxonomy in a fraction of the time and space required by the two-stage ensemble with which it was compared. However, generators and detectors are improving at a pace that may render these findings obsolete within a few years. Therefore, the value of this work lies as much in a protocol that can be repeated as in the numbers it reports today.
